opus-5.5.text:
I think this is actually one of the core difficulties right now, and it's quite different from the text-only case.

In language, when people did reinforcement learning on top of a pretrained model and saw these "aha moments" — reflection, backtracking, verifying intermediate steps — a big reason it worked is that those patterns already existed in the pretraining corpus. Humans write down their reasoning. Math solutions, forum discussions, textbooks: there's a lot of text where someone says "wait, that's wrong, let me try again." So RL isn't really inventing new cognitive behaviors; it's selecting and amplifying behaviors the model has already seen, and turning them from rare into reliable.

In vision, that foundation is much thinner. When a person solves a visual problem — say a maze, a geometry figure, or finding a specific object in a cluttered scene — the actual reasoning happens in their head. They look here, then there, mentally trace a path, zoom in on a region, imagine rotating something. Almost none of that process is recorded anywhere. What exists on the internet is mostly image-caption pairs: here's a picture, here's a description. That's perception-level alignment, not reasoning. So if you take a multimodal model and run RL on it, you often find the model just converts the image into text early and then reasons in language. That works for some tasks, but it hits a ceiling whenever the problem genuinely requires operating in visual space.

So the challenge becomes: how do you get a model to develop reasoning patterns that it has essentially never seen demonstrated? I see a few directions.

One is to construct the data yourself — synthesize trajectories where the model does things like cropping, marking, drawing auxiliary lines, or producing intermediate images, and use those to bootstrap the behavior before RL. The risk is that the patterns you design reflect your own assumptions, and they may not be the ones that actually scale.

Another is to rely more on exploration — give the model the right action space, such as tools to manipulate images or the ability to generate visual intermediate states, and let RL discover what's useful. But exploration from near-zero prior is very expensive. If the starting policy almost never produces a good trajectory, the reward signal is too sparse to learn anything.

A third, and I think more fundamental, direction is to fix the pretraining side — find or create data sources where visual thinking processes are actually captured. Video is interesting here, because it contains temporal processes, cause and effect, sometimes people demonstrating how to do something step by step. But extracting reasoning signal from video is still an open problem.

Honestly, my view is that we haven't yet found the visual equivalent of the "chain of thought" that's naturally abundant in text. Until we do, multimodal reasoning will lag behind language reasoning, and much of the apparent progress will really be language reasoning wearing a visual front end. Solving that gap — either through better data, better architectures that let models think in visual representations, or a smarter combination of synthesis and RL — is, to me, one of the most important open questions in the field.

r001.rationale: The response argues that multimodal systems need to develop visual reasoning patterns absent from pretraining, and discusses synthesis, exploration, and new data sources as ways to do so.

fable-5.1.text:
This is actually one of the problems I think about the most right now, and I'll be honest, I think it's a much deeper issue than most people in the field acknowledge.

Let me start with what happened in language. Why did reasoning work so well in LLMs, especially after o1 and R1? My view is that it's not that reinforcement learning taught the model to reason from scratch. The reasoning patterns were already in the pretraining data. Humans have written down, over thousands of years, enormous amounts of text where they reflect, they backtrack, they say "wait, let me reconsider," they verify their work. Textbooks, math forums, code reviews, Stack Overflow. The internet is full of human thinking processes expressed in words. So when you do RL on top of that, you're essentially amplifying and selecting behaviors that are latent in the base model. The patterns exist; RL just makes them reliable.

Now look at vision. Where is the "chain of thought" for visual perception on the internet? It basically doesn't exist. When a person looks at an image and figures something out, they don't write down "first I looked at the upper left corner, then I noticed the shadow was inconsistent with the light source, so I zoomed in." That process happens in our heads, it's almost never verbalized, and it's certainly never recorded at scale. Images on the internet come with captions, with alt text, with some descriptions, but almost never with the reasoning process that connects seeing to understanding.

So we have this fundamental asymmetry. For language, pretraining gave us the reasoning primitives for free. For vision, pretraining gives us recognition, gives us alignment between pixels and words, but it does not give us the primitives for visual reasoning. And this is why I think simply taking the LLM recipe, doing RL on a vision-language model with verifiable rewards, gives you something that looks like reasoning but is actually just language reasoning wearing a visual costume. The model converts the image into text tokens as early as possible, and then does all the real thinking in language space. The vision part is just a frontend.

You can see this empirically. If you look at the "thinking" traces of current multimodal reasoning models, almost all of the intermediate steps are textual. The model doesn't go back and look at the image again. It doesn't manipulate the image. It doesn't form a hypothesis and then check it against the pixels. It looks once, extracts what it can, and then reasons over that extraction. If the initial extraction is wrong or incomplete, the whole chain is built on sand.

So how do I think about solving this? A few directions, and I don't think any single one is sufficient.

The first is what I'd call native visual actions. If the reasoning patterns aren't in the data, maybe you can make them emerge through interaction. Give the model primitives like zoom, crop, compare, mark, and then let RL discover when to use them. The "thinking with images" line of work is a step in this direction. The hope is that if the action space is rich enough and the reward is right, the model will discover visual reasoning strategies that no human ever wrote down, the same way AlphaZero discovered chess ideas that weren't in any book. I think this is promising but there's a catch: the search space is huge and the reward signal is sparse, and unlike Go, we don't have a perfect simulator for "visual understanding." So in practice you end up relying heavily on cold-start data that humans construct, and now you're back to the question of whether humans can actually write down good visual reasoning traces. My experience is that it's really hard. Annotators produce something, but it's often not how they actually perceive.

The second direction, which I personally find more fundamental, is to question whether the reasoning has to happen in language at all. Maybe the right abstraction is reasoning in a latent visual space, or in a generative space. If a model can generate, it can imagine. It can render a hypothesis, "what would this scene look like from the other side," "what happens if I rotate this object," and then compare. Humans clearly do something like this, mental simulation, mental rotation. And crucially, generation gives you a form of self-verification that doesn't require words. I think the unification of understanding and generation is important not for product reasons but precisely for this reason: generation might be the missing substrate for visual reasoning, the way language is the substrate for symbolic reasoning. But I'll admit we're early here. Current unified models don't yet show clear evidence that generation improves understanding. That's still an open bet.

The third thing, and this is more of a hypothesis, is that we may be underestimating how much of the problem is scale and representation rather than algorithm. Part of why vision reasoning patterns seem absent is that our visual encoders are trained on contrastive or captioning objectives, which throw away most of the fine-grained information. The model literally cannot reason about things it has already discarded. So some of what looks like "missing reasoning patterns" is actually "missing information." If you fix the representation, if the encoder preserves enough that the model can go back and re-examine, then some reasoning behaviors become possible that simply weren't before.

If I zoom out, my honest assessment is: language reasoning got lucky. The data was there. For multimodal reasoning, we have to earn it, either by building environments where the patterns can be discovered, or by finding a different representational substrate where reasoning is natural. I don't think copying the text RL recipe will get us there. It'll get us better benchmarks, but I think it'll plateau in a way that's going to surprise people who expect it to just scale.

And one more thing, maybe the most important. We should be careful about what "reasoning" means in vision at all. In math, reasoning means multi-step derivation with verification. In vision, maybe the analogous thing isn't long chains of thought. Maybe it's something more like iterative attention, hypothesis and refinement, or active perception. If we force the visual problem into the shape of the language solution, we might be solving the wrong problem beautifully. So part of the challenge, honestly, is that we don't yet have a precise definition of what we're trying to produce. And I'd rather sit with that uncertainty than pretend the answer is obvious.

r001.rationale: The response argues that multimodal reasoning patterns are missing from pretraining and should be developed through interaction or alternative representational substrates, rather than limiting the system to patterns already present in its data.

astra-6.text:
I think the key challenge is that we want the model to discover useful ways of reasoning, but how does it know which new patterns are useful? If a pattern is absent from pretraining, simply asking the model to imitate more examples won’t solve the problem. You need some opportunity to explore, and feedback that tells it whether that exploration actually helped.

In a multimodal setting, that could mean learning when to look again at an image, when to focus on a particular region, or when to use a visual representation to check an intermediate conclusion. The reasoning is partly about deciding what information to acquire next, rather than just producing a longer explanation.

But I would distinguish a pattern that is genuinely beyond the model’s capabilities from one that it can construct by combining things it already knows. For the second case, exploration with reliable feedback seems promising. For the first, you may need additional training or a different interface to the environment.

So I would start with tasks where success is checkable, give the model room to try different strategies, and then test whether the strategies transfer. Otherwise, it’s very easy to reward something that looks like sophisticated reasoning without making the model more useful.

r001.rationale: The response says that patterns absent from pretraining require exploration and feedback, and describes learning new multimodal strategies rather than relying only on imitation of existing examples.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key challenge is that we want the model to discover a useful way of reasoning, but we may not have examples showing what that reasoning should look like. In a multimodal setting, that could mean deciding when to look at an image again, which region to inspect, or how to connect a visual observation with a symbolic calculation.

I would distinguish a pattern that is absent from the training data from one whose underlying ingredients are absent. If the model already has the basic perceptual and reasoning capabilities, it might learn to combine them in a new way. But if it cannot perceive the relevant information at all, asking it to reason longer won’t necessarily help.

So one promising approach is to create tasks where success is verifiable, allow the model to explore different strategies, and reward the ones that actually work. The hard part is making sure it learns a general strategy rather than a shortcut. You would want to test it on new situations where the same reasoning pattern is useful, but the surface details are different.

r001.rationale: The response says a model may learn to combine existing perceptual and reasoning capabilities in a new way even when examples of that reasoning pattern are absent from training data.
